title: Sweet Lick Knob: Fort Ancient Gathering Place
summary: In Estill County, Fort Ancient people used a large public building at the Sweet Lick Knob site from about 1400 to 1450 CE, likely for meetings.
bodyMarkdown:
Sometime around 1400 CE, Fort Ancient people in Estill County built a very large building. It wasn't a house. It stood about 42 feet long and 28 feet wide, with more than 1,176 square feet of floor. Down its center ran a line of three deep pits where tall poles had once stood, and two neat rectangular hearths.

For about fifty years, until about 1450, this building seems to have been a place where people came together.

The [Fort Ancient](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fort_Ancient) people were farmers who lived in the middle Ohio Valley from about 1000 CE until after Europeans arrived. Most of them lived in villages that were often circular, with houses ringed around a plaza. A single large public building with no village plan around it is unusual. University of Kentucky archaeologists dug the site in 2010.

They studied the building's size, what was inside it, what was found on its floor, and its radiocarbon dates, and concluded that it was a public building for social or ritual meetings that happened from time to time.

The pole pits tell part of the story. Each was about a foot and a half across and went more than two feet below the floor. Poles like these may have held sacred meaning.

At some point, the southern hearth and the southern pole pit were capped with clay at the same moment. This looks like a deliberate act, perhaps closing one part of the building's life.

People also worked here. The floor held every stage of making sandstone disks: rough stones chipped into circles, chipped again to make them smaller, then ground smooth. Disks like these may have been used in games such as [chunkey](https://grokipedia.com/page/Chunkey). The floor also held ornaments made of [cannel coal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cannel_coal), a shiny coal found in eastern Kentucky.

The site lies where two kinds of Fort Ancient country meet. To the east, most sites from this time are rockshelters, used by people who traveled and hunted in the mountains. To the west, most are large villages. Archaeologists think the hill itself, which can be seen from far away, may have worked like a beacon, drawing scattered groups together for ceremonies.

## Kentucky today

The site is protected, and its exact location stays off public maps to guard it from looting. It reminds us that Fort Ancient life in Estill County included more than farms and villages: there were also shared places where separate communities met. Learn about it from a distance, and support the archaeologists and descendant nations who look after places like it.
Source: [https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Sweet-Lick-Knob.aspx](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Sweet-Lick-Knob.aspx)
